question: Move the AED at P.S. 053 Basheer Quisim into a 24/7 outdoor cabinet on the building's street wall.

evidence.text: P.S. 053 Basheer Quisim (School, ZIP 10456) has a registered AED at "4th Floor Outside RM 406; Main Entrance Mini A; Main Entrance/ Main Bldg".
Its hours come from: School building assumed open 7 AM to 6 PM on school days, September to June. Move the school-hours control to test other closing times.
Under that assumption it is reachable 55 of 168 hours in a school-year week, and 0 hours in a summer week if it is a school.
In 2025, an expected 1.65 cardiac-arrest 911 calls a year came from inside its two-minute walking area at hours when every AED in reach was shut (rank 1 of 100 NYC schools).
Within 400 m there are 3 other registered AED locations; 0 of them are open 24/7 by their published hours.
Citywide, a time-blind map puts 4.6% of call-weighted area within a two-minute walk of an AED; at the hour calls actually came in, 1.4% was within reach of one confirmed open.
Published research: a bystander shock with a public AED was associated with survival to discharge of 66.5% versus 43.0% without (Pollack et al., Circulation 2018, observed shockable public arrests).
Overture Maps lists Engine 92 Ladder 44, a fire station normally staffed around the clock, 268 m away: a possible alternative host for a 24/7 AED.
Unknown to this data: cabinet cost, vandalism risk, whether the school already allows after-hours access, and the actual location of each 2025 call inside the ZIP (only ZIP-level data is public).

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: Moving this AED to a 24/7 outdoor cabinet directly addresses a documented gap. The school's current indoor placement is reachable only 55 of 168 hours weekly during the school year and zero hours in summer [E3], yet the area experienced 1.65 cardiac-arrest calls annually during times when every nearby AED was closed [E4]. This school ranks first among 100 NYC schools for this problem. Research shows bystander shock with a public AED correlates with 66.5% survival versus 43.0% without [E7]. The three other AEDs nearby aren't open 24/7 [E5], making this street-wall cabinet a practical way to close a real survival gap in a high-need area.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The proposal rests on incomplete data that may overstate the problem. While 1.65 annual calls in a closed-AED window sounds urgent [E4], we don't know where those calls actually occurred within the ZIP code [E9]—they could be blocks away from P.S. 053's street wall. The citywide baseline shows only 1.4% of call-weighted area reaches an open AED at call time [E6], so this school's rank reflects a broader system issue, not necessarily a site-specific crisis. Before installing an outdoor cabinet—whose cost and vandalism risk remain unknown [E9]—the council should explore whether Engine 92 Ladder 44, staffed around the clock just 268 meters away [E8], could host a 24/7 AED instead. That alternative avoids school liability and maintenance burden while serving the same two-minute radius.

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: The skeptic is right that we don't know the exact location of those 1.65 calls within the ZIP [E9], so we can't confirm they all fall within P.S. 053's two-minute radius. However, the school's rank-1 status among 100 NYC schools [E4] suggests a genuine concentration of need here, not random scatter. The fire station alternative at 268 meters [E8] deserves exploration, but it's unknown whether the FDNY would accept an AED or maintain it reliably. A school-wall cabinet puts the device directly in the community's hands during the 1.4% of call-weighted hours when the system currently fails [E6]. Without knowing cabinet costs or vandalism risk [E9], we can't rule out this option as impractical—and the survival benefit of accessible defibrillation [E7] argues for moving forward rather than waiting for a perfect alternative.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The Advocate is right that the fire station alternative remains untested and the school's rank-1 status suggests real concentration of need [E4]. But that ranking itself is ambiguous: we know only that 1.65 calls annually occurred in a closed-AED window somewhere in the ZIP, not that they cluster near P.S. 053's street wall [E9]. The citywide picture shows 1.4% of call-weighted area reaches an open AED at call time [E6]—this school may simply reflect that system-wide failure rather than a localized crisis. Before committing to an outdoor cabinet whose cost, maintenance, and vandalism exposure remain unknown [E9], the council should first contact Engine 92 Ladder 44 at 268 meters [E8]. If the FDNY declines, then revisit the school option with full cost data in hand.

verdict.summary: School ranks first among 100 NYC schools for cardiac-arrest calls during closed-AED hours [E4], but exact call locations within ZIP are unknown [E9]. Fire station alternative 268 m away [E8] should be explored before committing to outdoor cabinet whose cost and vandalism risk remain unquantified [E9].
verdict.strongestFor: Rank-1 problem density [E4], 66.5% survival with public AED [E7], current 55/168 weekly reachability [E3].
verdict.strongestAgainst: Call locations unknown within ZIP [E9], fire station alternative untested [E8], cabinet cost and vandalism risk unknown [E9].
verdict.nextStep: Contact Engine 92 Ladder 44 to assess 24/7 AED hosting feasibility; obtain cabinet cost and vandalism data before school decision.
